data.headline: Reading the tide before the trail
data.summary: A printed tide table, a pencil and ten minutes are what stand between a good day on the Black Rocks and an afternoon waiting on the headland.
data.imageAlt: Hands holding a printed tide table and a pencil over a barnacled rock on a wet beach.
data.caption: Marking the morning low water on the Black Rocks crossing.
data.body:
Every coastal trail on this site has a line about the tide, and every season someone reads it after setting out. The table is not hard to use. It lists two low waters and two high waters a day, about twelve and a half hours apart, and the time moves later by roughly fifty minutes each day.

For the Black Rocks the useful number is the morning low. Start walking at that time, cross the rock in the first hour, and the water is still well below the path when you reach the south cove. Start two hours later and the last hundred metres are under water.

Write the times on the back of your hand or on the map. Phones run out of battery on long days; a pencil note does not.

data.headline: The people who keep the steps
data.summary: A winter of Saturdays rebuilt the stone steps on the Ferns Falls trail. Three of the volunteers explain how.
data.imageAlt: Three volunteers in work gloves rebuilding stone steps on a forest trail, branches piled to one side.
data.caption: Resetting the lower steps on Ferns Falls in July.
data.body:
Water does most of the damage. A step that sheds rain to the side lasts for years; one that lets it run down the middle of the path loses its footing in a season. So the work starts with drainage: a stone set across the path at an angle, every ten metres on the steep sections.

The steps themselves are flat stones from the stream bed, set into the slope with their longest side buried. Twelve people worked on Saturdays from June to September and set one hundred and forty steps.

The trail office keeps a list of work days. Nobody needs experience, only gloves and closed shoes.

data.name: Wind Crest
data.summary: A granite ridge above the cloud line, with the whole coast in view on a clear morning.
data.imageAlt: A rocky ridge trail with a stone cairn above a sea of morning clouds.
data.body:
The trail leaves the village road at the chapel and climbs through pasture for the first hour, the last place with water. Above the treeline it follows the crest on bare granite, marked by cairns every hundred metres or so.

Start before seven: cloud tends to build on the crest after midday, and the cairns are hard to follow in it. Carry two litres of water, a wind layer and a headlamp. Turn back at the second saddle if the wind is strong enough to move you.

data.name: Black Rocks
data.summary: Dark coastal rock between two coves, passable only on a falling tide.
data.imageAlt: A trail across dark coastal rocks with tide pools and a wooden waymark post, a sandy cove beyond.

facts.label: Tide
facts.value: Cross the rocks within two hours of low water

data.body:
From the north cove the path crosses a kilometre of flat black rock to the south cove, then climbs over the headland on a forest track. Waymark posts stand on the rock where the line is not obvious.

The rock section floods at high tide. Leave the north cove no later than two hours after low water, and wear shoes that grip on wet rock. The headland path is dry in any weather.

data.name: Ferns Falls
data.summary: A shaded walk through the Atlantic forest to a small waterfall and a pool you can swim in.
data.imageAlt: A dirt path through dense green forest with ferns, a small waterfall and pool to one side.

facts.label: Season
facts.value: Best after rain, slippery for a day after it

data.body:
The path follows the stream up the valley under a closed canopy, so it stays cool even in January. Stone steps take it over the two steep sections; volunteers rebuilt them last winter.

The pool below the falls is deep enough to swim from March to May. Keep to the path near the bromeliads, which grow on the rocks at ankle height.

data.name: Marina Alves
data.summary: Leads the ridge and coastal trips and writes most of the trail notes.
data.imageAlt: A woman in a field shirt and cap standing on a grassy headland above the sea.
data.body:
Marina grew up in the village at the foot of Wind Crest and has walked its ridge in every month of the year. She trained as a wilderness first responder and checks every trail she leads in the week before a trip.

She writes the tide notes on this site and answers most of the questions that reach the trail office.

data.name: Wind Crest overnight
data.summary: Two days on the ridge with a night under the stars on the high saddle, for walkers who are comfortable with a long climb.
data.imageAlt: Small tents on a grassy saddle between peaks at dusk, hikers eating together by headlamp.

facts.label: Includes
facts.value: Shuttle, meals, tents and a guide

data.body:
Day one climbs Wind Crest from the chapel and camps on the high saddle, about five hours of walking. Day two follows the crest north at sunrise and descends to the village by early afternoon.

You carry your own clothes and sleeping bag; tents and food go up with the group and are shared out at the start. The trip runs if the forecast wind on the crest is below forty kilometres an hour, and otherwise moves to the next weekend.

data.heading: A brand made up to show a real product
data.body:
Quilhara is invented. The trails, places, guides, trips and stories on this site do not exist, and nothing here can be booked. It is a sample site for Viglet Shio, the open-source CMS, installed from one marketplace package.

The photographs were generated for the package and are free to redistribute with it. The fonts are Fraunces and Inter, both under the SIL Open Font Licence and served from the site itself.

data.heading: The trail office
data.body:
The office is a wooden hut at the edge of the village, open from eight to noon on weekdays. Trail conditions are posted on the noticeboard by the door before nine.

Write to trails@quilhara.example with the trail or trip you are asking about and the dates you have in mind. We answer within two working days.

data.heading: One package, three jobs
data.body:
Quilhara was installed from one marketplace package. An agent builds and maintains a Shio site, a curator approves what it did, and the content delivery API serves it. Each page below shows one part of that, on this site's own content.

  • How an agent reads this site
  • How the agent wrote it
  • How the agent proved it
  • What the curator did
  • The same site as files
  • The same content over REST and GraphQL
  • Where each image is used
  • How an existing site becomes an authorable one
  • Site search

Every page ends with the console screen, the MCP call, the CLI line and the delivery request behind it. They run against the instance you are reading, so you can copy one and try it.

data.title: How this site was built
data.description: The feature tour: which Shio capability each page of Quilhara shows, and how to do the same.

data.heading: Discovery is one call
data.body:
An agent that meets this instance for the first time asks for the context pack. It answers with every post type and its fields, the site's pages addressed by path, and the conventions an author here follows. Its manifest projection and capability list say which features this instance has switched on, and a digest lets the next session skip the read when nothing changed.

Pages are named by address, such as post:quilhara/trails/wind-crest, never by an id the agent would have to look up first. A read can ask for some fields only, a conditional read answers "unchanged" for nothing, and responses are terse by default. A request that goes wrong comes back with what to fix, what is allowed and an example, so the next call is the right one.

The same pack can be written out as project instructions (AGENTS.md), an agent can store a decision for the next session, and an agent token is scoped to the sites it may touch.

data.heading: Try it on this instance
data.mcpCall: shio_context {"site": "quilhara"}; shio_find {"site": "quilhara", "type": "Trail"}; shio_read {"address": "post:quilhara/trails/wind-crest", "fields": "name,facts"}; shio_remember {"site": "quilhara", "key": "voice", "note": "Field guide, not brochure"}

data.title: How an agent reads this site
data.description: One call returns the content model, the sitemap and the house rules, so an agent starts work without exploring.

data.heading: Desired state, applied twice with the same result
data.body:
Every page here was written as a desired-state document: the site, its post types and its posts, applied in one batch. Applying it again changes nothing, so a retry is safe. A dry run prints the plan first, and a destructive step, such as pruning a folder or deleting a site, needs a confirm token from that plan before it runs.

The package is a blueprint: the post types merge into whatever the instance already has, folders and posts can move without breaking their addresses, and each write answers with proof of what it stored. Nothing goes live until it is published, and publishing is its own call.

data.heading: Try it on this instance
data.mcpCall: shio_apply {"site": "quilhara", "blueprint": "quilhara", "dryRun": true}; shio_write {"address": "post:quilhara/trails/wind-crest", "data": {"summary": "A granite ridge above the clouds."}}; shio_publish {"address": "post:quilhara/trails/wind-crest"}

data.title: How the agent wrote it
data.description: Plans, batches and idempotent applies: how the pages of this site were written and published.

data.heading: Cheap proof instead of a screenshot
data.body:
Before this site was published, verify linted its content and its routes: empty required fields, references to nothing, two pages on one address, links that resolve nowhere. The render digest describes a page as text, its outline, landmarks, links and images, at a fraction of a screenshot's cost, and a page audit names what is wrong with a selector each.

The same checks run after every change. A change cursor says what happened since the last look, diagnostics and incidents survive a restart, a delivery proof fetches the published routes from the site's own address, and when a picture is needed a visual snapshot says whether the page looks different from last time.

data.title: How the agent proved it
data.description: Lint, route checks and render digests: proof in text that the site works, without anyone looking at it.

data.heading: The agent proposes, a person approves
data.body:
A curator opened these pages in the Universal Editor and changed text where it sits on the page. What the agent wrote waited in the review queue, and the curator's verdict on each item is recorded. The publish gate lists the checks a page passes before it goes live.

Publishing can be scheduled, and a release brings several pages live together. Every save keeps a revision, so an earlier version can be compared and restored, and a deleted page goes to the trash rather than away. A preview link shows a draft to someone without an account, for as long as the link lives.

What a curator may change is set per folder. This site's layouts and theme live in /theme, which the package locked to administrators when it was applied, so an editor can rewrite every page here and still cannot restyle the site by accident.

data.title: What the curator did
data.description: Edit in place, review what the agent left, schedule, and restore an earlier version.

data.heading: Files are the cheapest way to edit
data.body:
Each page of this site can be pulled to a file: frontmatter for its fields and Markdown for its body, with images as paths rather than ids. The post types are JSON files too, kept in version control next to the code that renders them.

Edit a file, push it, and a three-way merge applies only what changed; a field both sides changed is reported, not overwritten. A whole site also travels between instances as an exchange package.

data.title: The same site as files
data.description: Pull this site to disk as Markdown and JSON, edit it with ordinary tools, and push it back.

data.heading: One content store, several front ends
data.body: Shio renders this site itself, and the same content is open to any other front end. The REST delivery API reads a page by its address and language, lists a folder or a post type, and searches. GraphQL asks for exactly the fields a component needs. A webhook tells another system when a page is published, so a static build or a cache knows to refresh.

data.title: The same content over REST and GraphQL
data.description: Read these pages from any front end over REST or GraphQL, and hear about changes through webhooks.

data.heading: Images that know where they are
data.body:
The photographs on this site came in with the package, each with a description for someone who cannot see it. The asset list says which pages use each one, so an image nothing references can be found and removed, and one a page still needs is never deleted by mistake.

The listings serve each image in the sizes a card needs rather than the full original, and the story pages show the caption and alt text stored with the picture.

data.title: Where each image is used
data.description: Every photograph on this site, what it shows, which pages use it, and the sizes it is served in.

data.heading: Capture, propose, convert
data.body:
Quilhara was written for the package, but most sites already exist somewhere. Shio captures one by crawling it into an inventory of pages, markup and assets, and writes no content while it does. A proposal then names which repeated blocks could become sections and what each would lose.

Converting applies the accepted plan as drafts: post types for the sections, a theme from the captured styles, and pages a curator can edit. Nothing is published until someone reviews it.

data.title: How an existing site becomes an authorable one
data.description: Capture a site that already exists, choose which of its blocks become sections, and convert it as drafts.
